entries.title: [사설] 저궤도위성통신, 검토만 할 건가 - 전자신문
entries.paragraph_1: 정부가 지난 7월 '우주항공산업 육성전략'에 따라 2035년까지 최대 512기에 달하는 저궤도위성을 쏘아 올린다는 계획을 내놓았지만, 정작 이를 이행하기 위한 사전 절차는 더뎌도 너무 더딘 모습이다. 독자적인 저궤도 위성통신망을 구축하고 상용화하려면 궤도와 주파수 자원 확보가 필수적이다. 그러나 정작 첫 관문이자 단추라 할 수 있는 국제전기통신연합(ITU) 위성망 주파수 국제 등록 건수에서 한국은 고작 2건에 불과한 것으로 드러났다. 치열한 패권 다툼이 펼쳐지고 있는 글로벌 우주 영토 전쟁 현주소를 감안하면 어처구니가 없다. 현재 위성통신망 구축에 주로 활용되는 주파수는 Ku와 Ka 대역이다. 이 가운데 Ku 대역은 스페이스X의 스타링크, 원웹 등 글로벌 선두 주자들이 이미 수천, 수만 기의 위성을 쏘아 올리며 주파수를 사실상 독점해 신규 자원이 바닥난 실정이다. 남은 Ka 대역 역시 빠르게 채워지고 있다. 주요국과 글로벌 기업이 빠르게 선점하고 있기 때문이다. 이미 1년 전 기준으로 ITU Ka 대역 위성망 국제 등록 건수는 153건, 신청 위성 수만 해도 58만기를 넘어섰다. 주요국이 주파수와 궤도를 선점하기 위해 사력을 다하고 있는데, 한국은 2035년 상용화 개시란 타임라인만 세워둔 채 사실상 검토만 하고 있었으니 너무나 안이한 대응이 아닌가 묻지 않을 수 없다. 전문가 지적을 종합해 보면, 위성통신망 역시 지상 통신망과 마찬가지로 주파수 확보가 최우선 과제다. 특히 한국 저궤도위성통신 사업의 목적이 단순 내수용이 아니라 글로벌 통신 수요를 흡수하는 데 있다면 그 규모에 맞는 주파수 조기 확보가 필수 조건이다. 우선 정부와 사업자가 연합해 ITU 위성망 신청 절차를 밟고 이후 실제 위성 발사와 개국까지 이어지는 일련의 시간표를 최소 3~5년 이상 획기적으로 앞당기는 방법이 있다. 여기에 이미 주파수와 궤도를 확보해 운용 중이거나 등록을 마친 해외 위성국과 전략적인 협력 또는 공조 방안을 찾는 것이 남았다. 자원 인수나 공동 위성통신망 사업 추진 등 가능한 모든 옵션을 테이블 위에 올려놓고 저울질해야 한다. 저궤도 위성통신은 미래 6G 시대를 이끌 핵심 인프라이자 국가 안보와 산업 경쟁력의 집약체다. 언제까지 사업 검토와 예산·비용 확보를 위한 타당성 점검에는 소중한 시간을 허비할 것인지 걱정이 크다. 당장 오늘부터라도 정부와 사업자가 함께 머리를 맞대고, 우리의 명확한 목적과 현실에 부합하는 정밀한 실행 전략 마련에 나서길 바란다.

entries.title: Oakland Coal Terminal Backed by Trump Would Be Bigger, Dirtier Than Promised, Says Report | Post News Group
entries.paragraph_1: By Post Staff A recent feasibility study commissioned by potential investors says an Oakland coal terminal backed by President Donald Trump could export 13 million tons a year — three times the amount estimated in an earlier environmental review. Surprisingly, the report also contradicts developers’ and project advocates’ repeated pledges that the coal would be stored in a covered terminal. Instead, the millions of tons of coal shipped annually from inland states to the West Gateway terminal in Oakland would be stored in “two open-air bunkers,” with about 150,000 tons of coal per stockpile, before being sent overseas, according to the recent report cited by the L.A. Times. ( https://ruic.utah.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Port-Study-RUIC-Bulk-Commodity-Ocean-Terminals-Study.pdf ) Residents and clean air advocates have long expressed concerns that coal dust would worsen pollution in West Oakland and throughout the East Bay. The proposed site of the Oakland Bulk and Oversized Terminal (OBOT) is located at the former Army base near the Port of Oakland, which developer Phil Tagami has been trying for years to turn into a shipping terminal despite determined community opposition. Trump announced a $75-million investment in the project in June , about a third of its estimated cost. The new terminal would be the largest coal export site on the West Coast, transporting coal to Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam and Malaysia, according to the Trump administration. Trending Rockets Depth Proves Important in Playoffs Opponents say a new terminal would undermine years of progress cleaning up the air in West Oakland, which has a history of disproportionate pollution and high asthma rates due to its proximity to the port and other industry. According to No Coal in Oakland organizer Ted Franklin, who has been active for 11 years in the fight to stop the coal terminal, the report indicates that investors may be looking for a cheaper way to build the terminal. “We were shocked but not surprised” by the report, Franklin said. “Basically, it seems that the plan now is to store open piles of coal, which is a less expensive project than creating a completely enclosed facility.” The threats that the project poses are real, but it faces a lot of economic and legal hurdles, he said. Coal production is in permanent decline worldwide, he said, wondering who was going to “invest money in an industry that has no future.” Further, the project has not yet attracted big investors. “There’s no bank, no financing, no financial institution backing this,” he continued. A major legal hurdle facing the project is the passage of Assemblymember Mia Bonta’s bill, AB 40, the Community-First Coal Review Act, signed into law by Gov. Gavin Newsom on Sept. 30. The law requires developers of large-volume bulk coal facilities to complete a full Environmental Impact Report (EIR) under the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) before they can operate. The law was specifically designed to block or delay the coal terminal project. The report to potential developers was produced by consulting groups Norda Stelo and Wood Mackenzie in July and released this month. It was commissioned by the Rural Utah Infrastructure Coalition, made up of eight Utah counties that are considering investing about $43 million into the terminal to receive Utah coal. The consultants produced their findings after visiting Oakland, examining engineering documents and holding discussions with Savage Cos., a Utah-based transport and logistics company selected to operate the facility Research has shown that coal terminal operations can be dangerous to public health. The ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach moved away from open-air coal and petroleum coke storage three decades ago. The report says that the site could process 12 million metric tons, or 13.2 million tons, of coal each year, three times more than the terminal’s approved environmental impact report from 2002 and its 2012 addendum. Neither document mentions coal specifically, but rather bulk commodities. The coal arriving in Oakland could also be dirtier then had been previously stated, according to the report. Project officials previously said the terminal would handle only high-grade western bituminous coal from Utah, but the recent report says it will also handle Powder River Basin coal from Wyoming and Montana, known to be much dustier. Nor does the report mention plans to cover the rail cars to prevent pollution, though project officials previously promised they would only utilize coal transported in covered rail cars. “It appears the developers want to build something much bigger and more polluting than anything they previously revealed, either in court or to the West Oakland community,” said Colin O’Brien, deputy managing attorney at the nonprofit Earthjustice, speaking to the L.A. Times. The report indicates that the project may be much more expensive and take longer to complete than anticipated. The Energy Department estimates the terminal will cost about $231 million, but the report places the price at between $430 million and $625 million. The terminal will take 53 months to complete according to the report, significantly longer than Trump’s promise of exports beginning in 2028. entries.paragraph_2: By Post Staff A recent feasibility study commissioned by potential investors says an Oakland coal terminal backed by President Donald Trump could export 13 million tons a year — three times the amount estimated in an earlier environmental review. Surprisingly, the report also contradicts developers’ and project advocates’ repeated pledges that the coal would be stored in a covered terminal. Instead, the millions of tons of coal shipped annually from inland states to the West Gateway terminal in Oakland would be stored in “two open-air bunkers,” with about 150,000 tons of coal per stockpile, before being sent overseas, according to the recent report cited by the L.A. Times. ( https://ruic.utah.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Port-Study-RUIC-Bulk-Commodity-Ocean-Terminals-Study.pdf ) Residents and clean air advocates have long expressed concerns that coal dust would worsen pollution in West Oakland and throughout the East Bay. The proposed site of the Oakland Bulk and Oversized Terminal (OBOT) is located at the former Army base near the Port of Oakland, which developer Phil Tagami has been trying for years to turn into a shipping terminal despite determined community opposition. Trump announced a $75-million investment in the project in June , about a third of its estimated cost. The new terminal would be the largest coal export site on the West Coast, transporting coal to Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam and Malaysia, according to the Trump administration. Trending Rockets Depth Proves Important in Playoffs Opponents say a new terminal would undermine years of progress cleaning up the air in West Oakland, which has a history of disproportionate pollution and high asthma rates due to its proximity to the port and other industry. According to No Coal in Oakland organizer Ted Franklin, who has been active for 11 years in the fight to stop the coal terminal, the report indicates that investors may be looking for a cheaper way to build the terminal. “We were shocked but not surprised” by the report, Franklin said. “Basically, it seems that the plan now is to store open piles of coal, which is a less expensive project than creating a completely enclosed facility.” The threats that the project poses are real, but it faces a lot of economic and legal hurdles, he said. Coal production is in permanent decline worldwide, he said, wondering who was going to “invest money in an industry that has no future.” Further, the project has not yet attracted big investors. “There’s no bank, no financing, no financial institution backing this,” he continued. A major legal hurdle facing the project is the passage of Assemblymember Mia Bonta’s bill, AB 40, the Community-First Coal Review Act, signed into law by Gov. Gavin Newsom on Sept. 30. The law requires developers of large-volume bulk coal facilities to complete a full Environmental Impact Report (EIR) under the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) before they can operate. The law was specifically designed to block or delay the coal terminal project. The report to potential developers was produced by consulting groups Norda Stelo and Wood Mackenzie in July and released this month. It was commissioned by the Rural Utah Infrastructure Coalition, made up of eight Utah counties that are considering investing about $43 million into the terminal to receive Utah coal. The consultants produced their findings after visiting Oakland, examining engineering documents and holding discussions with Savage Cos., a Utah-based transport and logistics company selected to operate the facility Research has shown that coal terminal operations can be dangerous to public health. The ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach moved away from open-air coal and petroleum coke storage three decades ago. The report says that the site could process 12 million metric tons, or 13.2 million tons, of coal each year, three times more than the terminal’s approved environmental impact report from 2002 and its 2012 addendum. Neither document mentions coal specifically, but rather bulk commodities. The coal arriving in Oakland could also be dirtier then had been previously stated, according to the report. Project officials previously said the terminal would handle only high-grade western bituminous coal from Utah, but the recent report says it will also handle Powder River Basin coal from Wyoming and Montana, known to be much dustier. Nor does the report mention plans to cover the rail cars to prevent pollution, though project officials previously promised they would only utilize coal transported in covered rail cars. “It appears the developers want to build something much bigger and more polluting than anything they previously revealed, either in court or to the West Oakland community,” said Colin O’Brien, deputy managing attorney at the nonprofit Earthjustice, speaking to the L.A. Times. The report indicates that the project may be much more expensive and take longer to complete than anticipated. The Energy Department estimates the terminal will cost about $231 million, but the report places the price at between $430 million and $625 million. The terminal will take 53 months to complete according to the report, significantly longer than Trump’s promise of exports beginning in 2028. entries.title: Sullivan and Begich don't stand up to Trump's lies and bullying | Letters To Editor | newsminer.com
entries.paragraph_1: To the editor: I am a 77-year-old Alaska Native Vietnam veteran that will not be voting for Sen. Dan Sullivan or Rep. Nick Begich this November since neither candidate seem concerned about President Trump’s blatant lying and bullying. I understand congressional concern over political retaliation for speaking honestly, but kowtowing to the president is not a trait we need in Alaska’s Washington D.C. delegation. It’s disheartening to hear Sen. Sullivan and Rep. Begich reiterating White House talking points you know they don’t believe, just because they want to keep their jobs.
entries.paragraph_2: The current Congress is subservient and will never challenge the president or try to reclaim its separation of power responsibilities. The 2027 Congress needs to take back its authority that has been surrendered to the executive branch. This will not happen by electing Republicans. Now is the time to send a blunt message to Trump by refusing to vote Republican.

entries.title: From Soviet-era UAZ to Aurus limousines: Russian cars used by foreign leaders
entries.paragraph_1: For decades, Russian and Soviet automotive exports have served as more than just transportation tools for foreign heads of state; they have functioned as diplomatic instruments and, in some cases, enduring symbols of geopolitical alignment. From the rugged utility of the UAZ-469B to the modern prestige of the Aurus Senat, the interaction between Russian vehicle manufacturers and international leaders reveals a complex dynamic where engineering capability, political signaling, and logistical realities intersect.
entries.paragraph_2: The historical precedent for this relationship dates back to the Cold War, when the Soviet government gifted an open-top, rear-wheel-drive UAZ-469B, a vehicle originally designed for military command, to Kim Il-sung, the leader of North Korea. This gesture established a pattern of reliance that persisted through generations. In 2018, his grandson, Kim Jong-un, arrived at a summit with the South Korean leader in a heavily armored Mercedes-Maybach, a clear indicator of a shift in the preferred status symbols of the North Korean regime. However, reports indicate that the North Korean leader's private garage also contains new models of the UAZ Patriot, suggesting that the brand has retained a functional place in the national fleet despite the availability of German luxury alternatives.

As a foreign affairs reporter, I closely follow developments from the Ministry of Unification, the Foreign Ministry and the Defense Ministry, tracking shifts in diplomacy, military policy and North Korea’s evolving posture. My work focuses on the intersection of geopolitics, security and policy decisions shaping the Korean Peninsula. Earlier in my career, I also reported on South Korea’s financial sector, covering banking, markets and regulatory developments—experience that continues to inform my understanding of how economic policy intersects with national strategy.

entries.title: Moskva krivi Seul za loše odnose. Želi ponovno surađivati - Index.hr
entries.paragraph_1: RUSIJA bi pozdravila konkretne poteze Južne Koreje za obnovu bilateralnih odnosa, rekao je zamjenik ruskog ministra vanjskih poslova Andrej Rudenko. Rudenko je na brifingu za medije u Moskvi istaknuo da Rusija svoje odnose s drugim državama ne povezuje sa sukobom u Ukrajini.
entries.paragraph_2: "Primijetili smo da južnokorejske vlasti u nekim izjavama iskazuju želju za normalizacijom odnosa, ali istodobno navode da je to moguće tek nakon promjene geopolitičke situacije, to jest završetka sukoba u Ukrajini", kazao je. Dodao je da Moskva nije odgovorna za pogoršanje odnosa sa Seulom i odgovornost je prebacio na Južnu Koreju zbog njezine odluke da se pridruži sankcijama protiv Rusije.

entries.title: Exploring National Identity and Historical Memory in Japan-Korea Relations: Recommended Readings
entries.paragraph_1: For Japan and South Korea, history is not merely a record of events. It is also a political resource, a national inheritance, and occasionally a diplomatic weapon.
entries.paragraph_2: For recommended reading on Japan–Korea relations, the four books discussed below offer different entry points: Kan Kimura’s The Burden of the Past for historical disputes and diplomacy; Michael J. Seth’s A Concise History of Korea for broader historical context; and Anti-Japan Tribalism and The Comfort Women Hoax for controversial revisionist arguments that require critical reading. This article focuses on historical memory and Japan–South Korea relations rather than offering a comprehensive survey of the entire relationship.
